title: Turing machines: finite rules and unbounded tape
summary: Describe computation by finite read–write rules on an unbounded tape, prove that outputs are unique, and verify explicit halting and divergent machines.
abstract: To add one to a number written as a row of marks, a machine can scan to the first blank, add a mark, and return to the beginning. A Turing machine makes this procedure precise using finitely many control states and rules that read one tape cell, write a symbol, and move the head. Its tape has room in both directions, although only finitely many cells contain nonblank symbols at any stage. A fixed starting configuration determines a unique run, so it cannot lead to two different halting outputs. Every finite part of a run visits only a finite interval, yet a machine can continue forever, either moving into new cells or staying in one place. Explicit machines distinguish having finite instructions, having a well-defined output if computation stops, and actually terminating.
